title: Big Student Loan Changes Are Coming July 1—Are You Ready?
summary: If you have student loans or are about to borrow money for college, listen up! On July 1, some big changes are coming. First, if you're one of the 7 million people using the SAVE repayment plan, you'll have to switch to a different plan. SAVE was a plan that let people with low incomes pay $0 a month. If you don't pick a new plan, the government will put you in one that might cost more. Experts worry this could cause more people to fall behind on their loans. There are new repayment plans to choose from, like the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) and the Tiered Standard Plan. You can use a loan simulator to see which is best for you. Also, starting July 1, if you're a graduate student, you can't borrow as much money as before. The new limit is $20,500 a year and $100,000 total. Some professional degrees, like doctors and lawyers, can borrow more—up to $50,000 a year and $200,000 total. If you're an undergrad, the limits haven't changed. These rules only affect new loans taken out on or after July 1. So if you're planning to borrow more for school, make sure you understand the new rules!
why_it_matters: If someone in your family is going to college, these rules might change how they pay for school, so understanding loans early can help you make smarter choices later.

background_read: The U.S. government gives student loans to help people pay for college or university.
The SAVE repayment plan was created in 2023 to help borrowers with low incomes pay little or nothing each month.
Now, because of new rules, the SAVE plan is ending, and 7 million people will have to switch to other plans like RAP or the Tiered Standard Plan.
Article_Structure: WHO: 7 million student loan borrowers in the SAVE plan, along with graduate, professional, and undergraduate students who take out new loans after July 1.
WHAT: The SAVE plan stops being available; new repayment plans like RAP and Tiered Standard appear; graduate and professional student borrowing limits are capped.
WHERE: Throughout the U.S. federal student loan system, which affects every college student who uses government loans.
WHY: The government is changing policies to update repayment choices and set new caps, which experts fear could cause more borrowers to struggle.

perspectives.description: New plans like RAP could give some borrowers a payment schedule that fits their budget better than the old options.
Losing the $0-a-month payment and being moved into a more expensive plan might cause many people to fall behind on their loans.
These changes only apply to new loans taken out on or after July 1, so families who already borrowed aren't immediately affected.
